title: Λέων καὶ ἄρκτος καὶ ἀλώπηξ
titleEn: The Lion, the Bear, and the Fox
part: The Lion, the Bear, and the Fox (Chambry 200)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 200. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λέων καὶ ἄρκτος, ἐλάφου νεβρὸν εὑρόντες, περὶ τούτου ἐμάχοντο.
sentences.tr: Leōn kai arktos, elaphou nebron heurontes, peri toutou emachonto.
sentences.l: A lion and a bear, having found a deer's fawn, were fighting over it.

sentences.t: Δεινῶς δὲ ὑπ’ ἀλλήλων διατεθέντες, ἐπειδὴ ἐσκοτώθησαν, ἡμιθανεῖς ἔκειντο.
sentences.tr: Deinōs de hyp’ allēlōn diatethentes, epeidē eskotōthēsan, hēmithaneis ekeinto.
sentences.l: And having been terribly handled by one another, when their sight went dark, they lay half-dead.
sentences.i: Mauled dreadfully by one another, they blacked out and lay there half dead.
sentences.n: δεινῶς διατεθέντες is idiomatic: διατίθημι in the passive is to be put into a state, and with δεινῶς it means to be badly used. σκοτόομαι, 'to be darkened', is what happens to a man's sight when he faints — the Greek describes the collapse from inside.

sentences.t: Ἀλώπηξ δὲ παριοῦσα, ὡς ἐθεάσατο τοὺς μὲν παρειμένους, τὸν δὲ νεβρὸν ἐν μέσῳ κείμενον, ἀραμένη αὐτόν, διὰ μέσων αὐτῶν ἀπηλλάττετο.
sentences.tr: Alōpēx de pariousa, hōs etheasato tous men pareimenous, ton de nebron en mesōi keimenon, aramenē auton, dia mesōn autōn apēllatteto.
sentences.l: And a fox passing by, when she saw the two of them gone slack and the fawn lying in the middle, having taken it up, made off right between them.
sentences.i: A fox going past saw the pair of them limp, and the fawn lying between, and picked it up and went off straight between them.
sentences.n: παρειμένους is the perfect passive participle of παρίημι, 'let go slack' — the word for limbs that have stopped answering. μέν and δέ set the two motionless beasts against the one motionless prize; διὰ μέσων αὐτῶν then picks the word up again and walks the fox through it.

sentences.t: Οἱ δὲ ἐξαναστῆναι μὴ δυνάμενοι ἔφασαν· « Ἄθλιοι ἡμεῖς, εἴ γε ἀλώπεκι ἐμοχθοῦμεν. »
sentences.tr: Hoi de exanastēnai mē dynamenoi ephasan· « Athlioi hēmeis, ei ge alōpeki emochthoumen. »
sentences.l: And they, not being able to get up, said: « Wretched are we, if indeed we have been toiling for a fox. »
sentences.i: And they, unable to rise, said: « Wretched creatures that we are, if all our labour has been for a fox. »
sentences.n: ἀλώπεκι is a dative of the person benefited: the toil was done, as it turns out, on the fox's behalf. εἴ γε concedes the fact while flinching from it, and the imperfect ἐμοχθοῦμεν looks back over the whole fight at once.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι εὐλόγως ἐκεῖνοι ἄχθονται οἳ τῶν ἰδίων πόνων τοὺς τυχόντας ὁρῶσι τὰς ἐπικαρπίας ἀποφερομένους.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti eulogōs ekeinoi achthontai hoi tōn idiōn ponōn tous tychontas horōsi tas epikarpias apopheromenous.
sentences.l: The story shows that with good reason those men are vexed who see chance comers carrying off the fruits of their own labours.
sentences.n: οἱ τυχόντες are 'whoever happens along', the first comers, people with no claim of their own. ἐπικαρπία is the yield a thing brings in, the crop as distinct from the field. ὁράω with a supplementary participle (ἀποφερομένους) reports what is actually seen happening, not merely learned.
